items.title: Interactive refactoring in gopls
items.author: Hongxiang Jiang
items.content:
When editing code in a modern IDE or editor, developers rely on its refactoring features to automate common transformations. Today, we are excited to introduce in gopls, powered by a new capability we are proposing for the Language Server Protocol (LSP) that brings dynamic, multi-step dialogs directly into your favorite editor. Crucially, we designed this capability (in collaboration with the Dart team) not just for Go, but as an open standard for all programming languages and editor ecosystems. Working support is already available in gopls v0.24.0 and the official Go extension for VS Code v0.56.0.

What is the Language Server Protocol (LSP)?

The LSP is an open standard that decouples language-specific features from specific text editors. As you navigate and edit code, your editor (such as VS Code, Neovim, or Emacs) and a language server (like gopls) engage in a continuous JSON-RPC exchange to provide features like autocomplete, hover documentation, diagnostics, and code actions.

Today, almost every code transformation in the LSP is like a function of no parameters: you trigger the operation, and the server immediately computes the edits. (Renaming a symbol is the sole exception: because it is a function of one parameter, the desired new name, it required its own dedicated RPC in the protocol.)

The language server must deduce the user’s intent from context alone, namely the cursor position and the enclosing syntax tree. When that context is not enough, the server is forced into one of two choices: apply a one-size-fits-all default, or refrain from offering the transformation altogether. The limitation lies not in gopls’s ability to compute the necessary edits, but in the LSP’s lack of a mechanism for language servers to ask the user for input.

For many transformations, this parameterless model works well. But many others need additional input from the user: which struct tags to add and in what naming convention, which interface to implement, which file to move a declaration to. Without a way to ask, gopls could only guess—“Add struct tags”, for example, always produced tags in —or not offer the refactoring at all. With interactive refactoring, language servers can now easily provide new operations with one or more parameters.

While some language extensions have worked around this limitation by embedding custom, language-specific dialog logic directly into individual editors, doing so leaves behind other editors (such as Neovim and Emacs) that stick strictly to the LSP with minimal custom client code. More importantly, editor-specific workarounds go against the fundamental purpose of the LSP: to decouple language-specific features from editors so that each server improvement benefits every client.

Interactive refactorings in action

Adding and removing struct tags (gopls v0.23.0)

When configuring serialization formats, developers frequently need custom tags and casing conventions. Previously, running “Add struct tags” unconditionally injected tags using formatting.

With interactive refactoring:

  1. Place your cursor on any struct definition and select the code action.
  2. An input dialog appears, pre-filled with , allowing you to customize any combination of tags (such as ).
  3. A second dialog lets you select your desired naming convention (such as , , or ).
  4. Gopls generates and applies the formatted struct tags across your type definition.

Here is the before-and-after transformation:

type UserProfile struct {
    ID        int64
    FirstName string
    LastName  string
    EmailAddr string
}

type UserProfile struct {
    ID        int64  `json:"id" db:"id"`
    FirstName string `json:"first_name" db:"first_name"`
    LastName  string `json:"last_name" db:"last_name"`
    EmailAddr string `json:"email_addr" db:"email_addr"`
}

Similarly, now asks you for the specific tag keys you wish to delete (for example, removing only tags while preserving the tag), rather than wiping out all struct tags indiscriminately.

Implementing interfaces with dynamic symbol search

When creating a type to satisfy an interface, developers previously had to copy the interface declaration and manually turn it into a set of methods on the receiver type (or rely on external tools like by manually typing the receiver and qualifying the name of the interface).

Since gopls v0.23.0, with interactive refactoring:

  1. Place your cursor on any concrete type and select the “Add methods to X to implement an interface…” code action.
  2. A text entry field appears, inviting you to choose the name of an interface type. It makes dynamic queries to gopls to auto-complete names of types in your workspace and the standard library (for example, ).
  3. If the selected interface has type parameters, gopls asks for a concrete type argument for each type parameter (such as ).
  4. Gopls generates complete method stubs with appropriate receiver names and instantiated method signatures.
type Foo struct{}

type MyHasher struct{}

type Foo struct{}

type MyHasher struct{}

// Equal implements [maphash.Hasher].
func (m *MyHasher) Equal(x Foo, y Foo) bool {
    panic("unimplemented")
}

// Hash implements [maphash.Hasher].
func (m *MyHasher) Hash(*maphash.Hash, Foo) {
    panic("unimplemented")
}

Moving declarations across files and packages (preview)

Moving declarations manually by cutting and pasting can easily break references and requires tedious import cleanup across multiple files. While scheduled for an upcoming gopls release, our working implementation already demonstrates how interactive file selection streamlines cross-file and cross-package moves:

  1. Place your cursor on any top-level declaration and select the code action.
  2. A file picker dialog lets you choose an existing destination file or specify a new file path.
  3. Gopls moves the declaration along with its dependent declarations (such as unexported helpers or methods) while leaving unrelated symbols in place, updates references across your workspace, and cleans up imports in both the source and destination files.

In the example below, we move the type from package to package . Its method and the unexported constant , which only uses, move along with it, while the unrelated function stays behind:

// from/from.go
package from

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

const bar = "bar"

// Doc comment for Foo
type Foo struct{}

func (f Foo) Print() {
    fmt.Println(bar)
}

func Baz() string {
    return strings.ToUpper("baz")
}

// from/from.go
package from

import "strings"

func Baz() string {
    return strings.ToUpper("baz")
}

// to/to.go
package to

import "fmt"

const bar = "bar"

// Doc comment for Foo
type Foo struct{}

func (f Foo) Print() {
    fmt.Println(bar)
}

Slaying the dragon (gopls v0.24.0)

As a demonstration of multi-step interactive dialogs and a self-contained test case for client editor implementations, gopls v0.24.0 offers a code action when you place your cursor on a package-level variable named (for example, ). Happy hunting!

Interactive refactoring establishes a foundational capability in gopls, opening up several exciting directions on our roadmap:

  • Change signature refactoring (#38028): Adding, removing, or reordering function parameters across a workspace requires input that cannot be deduced from syntax alone, such as the new parameter order or the default argument expression to insert at existing call sites. Interactive forms allow gopls to collect these details before rewriting the declaration and all call sites.
  • Interactive conflict resolution: When a code transformation encounters naming collisions, identifier shadowing, or ambiguous references, gopls can ask the user for guidance, such as asking for permission to proceed or offering to rename conflicting symbols on the fly.
  • Interactive commands beyond code edits: Because interactivity is modeled at the LSP command layer, it naturally generalizes to non-edit server operations that require user configuration, such as configuring test or benchmark runs with profiling flags (CPU, memory, tracing).

Getting Started and Sharing Feedback

Interactive refactoring is available in gopls v0.24.0 and v0.56.0 (with proof-of-concept client integrations also explored for Neovim and Emacs).

We would love to hear your thoughts as we continue refining interactive code actions in gopls:

(Special thanks to Alan Donovan, Alex Putman, Brian Wilkerson, Danny Tuppeny, Hana Kim, Madeline Kalil, Peter Weinberger, and Robert Findley for their insights, discussions, feedback, and collaboration on this work.)

items.title: Announcing Rust 1.99.1
items.author: The Rust Release Team
items.content:
The Rust team has published a new point release of Rust, 1.99.1. Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.99.1 is as easy as:

If you don't have it already, you can get from the appropriate page on our website.

Rust 1.99.1 fixes the following regressions from prior releases:

  • Missing symbol : Some Rust targets were getting link errors for missing , and that function is now present in Rust's compiler-builtins library as a fallback.

    The LLVM pass may introduce calls to as an optimization, and some Rust targets did not have that function readily available in or elsewhere. The UEFI targets in particular were broken for any project using , as some of these calls were introduced in the precompiled standard library, but the issue was also reproducible for similar user code patterns.

  • Miscompilation of FFI return values on x86_64: Rust functions returning through FFI could leave bits 1-7 of the return register unspecified, causing callers to observe raw values other than or . This return type is now marked for zero-extension again, as required by the ABI.

  • failed to load on macOS: This linker could fail to run if the compiler was invoked without the proxy, as there was no direct setting for the appropriate library search path. Now is built with an entry for the directory containing .

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider using the beta () and nightly () channels locally and in your CI. Please report any bugs you might come across!

Many people came together to create Rust 1.99.1. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

items.title: Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
items.content:
You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect.

In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?”

The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort.

This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example.

The alpha release provides read-only views for Kueue Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues, ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions allow them.

First, separate admission from Pod scheduling

Kueue and the Kubernetes scheduler answer different questions.

  • Kueue admission: Should this Workload start now, considering queue policy, quota, ResourceFlavors, admission checks, and other waiting Workloads?

  • Pod scheduling: After the Workload is admitted and the Job resumes, which nodes can run its Pods?

That boundary changes the investigation. If the Workload is not admitted, stay in the Kueue section of Headlamp. If it is admitted but its Pods are still , move to Headlamp's normal Job and Pod views and inspect scheduler events.

The Headlamp-first troubleshooting path

The quickest investigation starts with the Workload, not with a shell.

Step 1: Open the Workloads view

In Headlamp, open . Select the namespace that contains the Job, then find the Workload created for it.

Kueue creates a Workload to represent the resource request and admission state of a Job. In the alpha plugin, owner references are shown as text but are not yet clickable. The Workload name normally contains the Job name, so the namespace filter and table search are the simplest ways to locate it.

Before opening the detail page, the list already gives you a useful first scan:

  • priority and priority class

  • a readable current status such as , , or

If there is no matching Workload, check three things before going further: the selected namespace, whether the Job was submitted to a LocalQueue, and whether your Kubernetes account can list Workloads. The plugin performs permission checks and displays an access message when the current identity cannot read a resource.

Step 2: Read status, conditions, and events

Open the Workload. Start with its current status and conditions, not with the full YAML.

For admission troubleshooting, the most important condition types are and .

  • means Kueue has admitted the Workload. The Job can resume, so any remaining Pods belong to the scheduling branch of the investigation.

  • with a reason such as means Kueue has not reserved quota. The condition message explains what prevented the reservation.

  • An status means the Workload currently cannot fit the available queue configuration. A missing covered resource, unsuitable ResourceFlavor, stopped queue, or admission check can all lead you here.

For example, a condition message may report that Kueue could not assign a ResourceFlavor because the ClusterQueue has insufficient CPU quota. That message is the first real answer to “Why is my Job still pending?” The rest of the Headlamp journey explains the configuration behind it.

Also check the section. Conditions describe the current state; events help show what recently changed or what Kueue attempted.

Stay on the Workload detail page and inspect the PodSets and resource requests. The plugin shows the requested Pod count, CPU, memory, and other resources that Kueue evaluates together.

This matters because a Job with and a one-CPU request per Pod asks Kueue for three CPUs in total. Looking at only one Pod's template would underestimate the Workload.

If quota has already been reserved, the same page also shows the assigned ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavors, and admitted resource usage. If those admission assignments are absent, the Workload has not reached that point yet.

In our example, the Workload requests:

  • 600 MiB of memory in total

The next question is where that request entered Kueue.

Step 4: Follow the linked LocalQueue

Use the LocalQueue link on the Workload detail page. A LocalQueue is the namespace-level entry point used by the Job. It connects namespaced Workloads to a cluster-scoped ClusterQueue.

The LocalQueue page shows:

  • its namespace and connected ClusterQueue

  • stop policy and current status

  • pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts

  • Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events

  • related Workloads in the same namespace

This page answers two practical questions: Did the Job enter the queue you expected, and is it the only Workload waiting there?

If the LocalQueue is inactive or stopped, that may already explain the wait. If it is active, follow the linked ClusterQueue to inspect the capacity behind it.

Step 5: Inspect ClusterQueue capacity and usage

A ClusterQueue represents the cluster-level quota and admission policy available to one or more LocalQueues.

On its Headlamp detail page, compare the Workload request with:

  • nominal quota for each ResourceFlavor

  • current reservations and usage

  • borrowing and lending limits

  • pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts

  • queueing strategy and stop policy

  • preemption, fair-sharing, flavor-fungibility, and admission-check settings

  • Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events

For the example in this article, the ClusterQueue provides a nominal quota of two CPUs and two Pod slots. The Workload asks for three of each. The condition message and the ClusterQueue page now tell the same story: the Workload does not fit, so Kueue leaves the Job suspended.

This is an admission-capacity problem. It is not evidence that kube-scheduler failed to find a node.

Step 6: Check ResourceFlavor and Cohort when needed

Quota is not always a single pool. A ResourceFlavor can represent a class of compute through node labels, taints, tolerations, or topology settings. Use the ResourceFlavor link from the ClusterQueue when the condition mentions flavor assignment or when the Workload requires a particular hardware class, such as GPU nodes.

If the ClusterQueue belongs to a Cohort, follow that link too. Cohorts let ClusterQueues share unused quota. The Headlamp page shows parent and child Cohorts, member ClusterQueues, referenced ResourceFlavors, resource groups, borrowing and lending limits, and fair-sharing information.

These pages help answer a more subtle question: Is the Workload blocked because the queue has no quota of its own, because it cannot borrow enough, or because no suitable flavor can be assigned?

What we learned without leaving Headlamp

For the sample pending Job, the UI gives us a complete explanation:

  1. The Workload is not admitted.

  2. Its condition is false and the message points to insufficient quota.

  3. The Workload requests three CPUs and three Pod slots.

  4. Its LocalQueue is active and points to the expected ClusterQueue.

  5. The ClusterQueue provides only two CPUs and two Pod slots.

  6. Kueue therefore keeps the Job suspended until quota becomes available or the queue configuration changes.

The important part is not that Headlamp invents a new status. It reads the same Kubernetes API objects as other clients, then places the related resources and human-readable values in one connected investigation.

If the Workload is admitted, switch views

Suppose the Workload detail page shows , but the application is still not running. Kueue has completed its part of the decision. Continue in Headlamp's standard Kubernetes views:

  1. Open and inspect the Job state and events.

  2. Open and filter by the Job name or namespace.

  3. Select a Pod and read its section.

At this stage, look for scheduler concerns such as insufficient node capacity, node affinity, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, persistent-volume binding, or image-pull failures.

This handoff is the most useful troubleshooting rule in the article:

  • Not admitted: investigate Kueue resources in Headlamp.

  • , but Pods are : investigate Job, Pod, node, and scheduler information in Headlamp.

A repeatable Headlamp checklist

When the next Job does not start, use this short path:

  1. Open and select the correct namespace.

  2. Find the Workload associated with the Job.

  3. Check the readable status, , and conditions.

  4. Read the condition message and recent events.

  5. Compare PodSet resource requests with any admission assignments.

  6. Follow the LocalQueue link and confirm its status and ClusterQueue.

  7. Follow the ClusterQueue link and compare quota, reservations, usage, and policy.

  8. Inspect ResourceFlavor or Cohort details when the message points to flavor selection or shared quota.

  9. If admitted, move to Headlamp's Job and Pod views.

What Headlamp replaces during this investigation

The plugin does not replace or for scripts, exact object output, or changes. It replaces the repetitive UI-less navigation needed during an interactive investigation.

Is the Workload admitted?Kueue → Workloads → status and conditionskubectl describe workload <workload-name> -n <namespace>
Which LocalQueue did it enter?Workload → linked LocalQueuekubectl get localqueue <localqueue-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml
Which ClusterQueue provides quota?LocalQueue → linked ClusterQueuekubectl get clusterqueue <clusterqueue-name> -o yaml
Which flavor or shared quota matters?ClusterQueue → ResourceFlavor or Cohortkubectl get resourceflavor <flavor-name> -o yaml or kubectl get cohort <cohort-name> -o yaml
What happened after admission?Workloads → Jobs and Pods → eventskubectl describe job <job-name> -n <namespace> or kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>

For scripts and GitOps workflows, the command line remains the right tool. For a person asking “why is this waiting?”, the linked Headlamp path is usually faster to read.

Optional: reproduce the pending scenario

To reproduce the specific quota mismatch used in this article, configure a ClusterQueue with two CPUs and two Pod slots, then submit a three-Pod Job that requests one CPU per Pod. The Job enters its LocalQueue, Kueue creates a Workload, and the Workload remains pending because the combined request is larger than the available quota.

Keeping this setup separate from the main walkthrough is intentional: once the resources exist, the investigation itself should happen in Headlamp.

Current alpha limitations

The release is an initial read-only view of the Kueue admission path.

  • The plugin does not add its own create, edit, pause, resume, or delete flows.

  • Workload owner references are displayed as text and are not currently navigable.

  • The UI depends on the Kubernetes permissions of the identity used by Headlamp.

  • Metrics and a visual relationship map are possible follow-up areas rather than features of this release.

These limits are useful to state clearly: the plugin's current purpose is to make admission state and resource relationships easier to inspect.

Developed during LFX Mentorship

The plugin was developed during CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 using TypeScript, React, Kubernetes APIs, and Headlamp's plugin system.

Utkarsh Raj implemented the plugin with guidance and review from René Dudfield (@illume) and Kevin Hannon (@kannon92). Feedback from the Headlamp and Kueue communities shaped the resource views, status presentation, navigation, documentation, tests, and first alpha release.

Try it and share feedback

If a pending Workload is still difficult to explain after following the Headlamp path, that is exactly the kind of feedback that can improve the plugin.

items.title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse
items.author: Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil
items.content:
Take a look at the following function:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

It sends a request to and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 (), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible?

The cost of establishing HTTP connections

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request.

Go’s package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

  1. : the client sends a packet, the server replies with , and the client replies with . Because the client can send the first TLS message alongside that final , establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).
  2. : next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.
  3. : with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent after a total of 3 RTT.

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be expensive. Our opening benchmark queries index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable.

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

  • : while not part of the official specification, clients and servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header or sends a header.
  • : connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by sending a header.
  • : multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single TCP connection.

When connection reuse fails

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two requests are sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate , then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from .

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream, can only find the start of the next response after the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the or header).

Now look back at our example program, where we never read :

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Through Go 1.26, when is called, sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing the connection.)

Where failed connection reuse hurts

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they stop just short of the end of the body. For example, stops reading as soon as it sees the closing of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though it was only a single byte away from being reusable.

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years, many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body)
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it.
    body.Close()
}

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to drain:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
    body.Close()
}

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also need to cap the time we spend draining:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
    select {
    case <-drainDone:
    case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
        // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the
        // io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
    }
    body.Close()
}

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background and let it race against subsequent requests:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
    drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
    go func() {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
        drainDone <- struct{}{}
    }()
    go func() {
        // Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
        select {
        case <-drainDone:
            // If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the
            // connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is
            // created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of
            // idle connections, potentially being reused for another future
            // request.
        case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
            // If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt
            // the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
        }
        body.Close()
    }()
}

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary.

The current state and conclusion

Starting in Go 1.27, automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB. It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response contains the header, draining the body is guaranteed to be wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.

As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let deal with the complexities on your behalf.

items.title: The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
items.content:
In Linux, (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25.

Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features.

If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup.

For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The preflight check, provided by , returns an error during , , and when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details.

The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks, and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2.

Limitations of cgroup v1 and Improvements with cgroup v2

The Linux kernel documentation describes both interfaces:

Let's enumerate some known issues.

memory is not considered available memory

The kubelet treats memory as not reclaimable. For I/O-intensive workloads, a large page cache can therefore make the kubelet report memory pressure and evict Pods. This is a known kubelet issue (kubernetes/kubernetes#43916); migrating to cgroup v2 does not by itself change that calculation. The documented workaround is to set equal memory requests and limits for containers that perform intensive I/O, after measuring an appropriate value.

Memory QoS updates in Kubernetes v1.36

Memory QoS was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes v1.22 and updated in v1.27. It remains alpha in v1.36, but now separates memory throttling from memory reservation and adds tiered memory protection:

Memory QoS is available on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2. It relies on the cgroup v2 memory controller: provides throttling, while and provide hard and soft protection when tiered reservation is enabled. cgroup v1 cannot provide this protection model.

  • Enabling the feature gate applies throttling to Burstable containers. The threshold is derived from the request, limit, and (default ).

  • memoryReservationPolicy: None is the default. It does not write or .

  • memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation maps Guaranteed Pod memory requests to (hard protection) and Burstable Pod requests to (soft protection). BestEffort Pods receive neither protection.

  • The kubelet exposes Alpha metrics for the total and reservations on a node.

  • Kernel 5.9 or later is recommended. On older kernels, reclaim can trigger a known livelock; from v1.36 the kubelet logs a warning when Memory QoS is enabled on an affected kernel.

For example, to opt in to tiered protection:

The overall Kubernetes recommendation is not to enable Alpha features in production; however, if you judge that memory QoS with tiered reservations is useful for your platform in production, make sure to test the configuration account for hard-reserved memory before you enable the feature gate. See the Pod QoS documentation for the current mapping of Kubernetes QoS classes to cgroup v2 controls.

Container-aware OOM handling

On cgroup v2 nodes, the kubelet defaults to . It therefore sets for each container cgroup so that an OOM event kills all processes in that container together, rather than leaving a partially functioning multi-process container. Set singleProcessOOMKill: true only if you need the cgroup v1-compatible behavior where the kernel may kill one process at a time. See the reference for this setting.

This behavior is scoped to a container cgroup, not the whole Pod. Also, is a separate administrative interface: writing to it sends to every process in that cgroup and its descendants; it does not configure OOM behavior. The cgroup v2 memory controller additionally provides counters that monitoring systems and userspace OOM managers can observe.

In cgroup v1, delegating controllers to less privileged containers may be dangerous.

Unlike cgroup v1, cgroup v2 officially supports delegation. Most implementations of rootless containers rely on systemd for delegating v2 controllers to non-root users.

This delegation mechanism is separate from Kubernetes Pod user namespaces, which map container users to unprivileged host users. Pod user namespace support graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.36; check its filesystem, kernel, CRI runtime, and OCI runtime prerequisites before enabling it.

  1. eBPF stories:
    • In cgroup v1, device access controls are exposed through interface files.
    • The cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files, and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF.
    • Cilium attaches BPF cgroup programs for socket-based load balancing. Its default cgroup root is .
  2. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) reports CPU, memory, and I/O contention at node, Pod, and container level. On supported clusters, the kubelet exposes PSI by default ( is stable and locked on). PSI requires cgroup v2, Linux 4.20 or later, , and a kernel not booted with . The kubelet surfaces the data through the Summary API and .
  3. When migrating, update software that reads the cgroup filesystem directly. The migration guidance recommends cAdvisor v0.43.0 or later and lists compatible Java, Node.js, and versions.

CPU weight conversion in newer OCI runtimes

cgroup v1 uses , whereas cgroup v2 uses . Newer OCI runtimes use an improved non-linear conversion that preserves the default priority and gives small CPU requests more usable granularity. The change is implemented in the OCI runtime rather than Kubernetes: it is available in crun v1.23 and runc v1.3.2. After upgrading a runtime, monitoring or policy tools that predict exact values may need updates. Read New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight for the formula, examples, and compatibility considerations.

In-place resource updates

In-place Pod vertical scaling graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.35. Kubernetes v1.36 then [enabled] (/blog/2026/04/30/kubernetes-v1-36-inplace-pod-level-resources-beta/) in-place vertical scaling for Pod-level resources by default, as a Beta feature. The kubelet coordinates changes between the Pod-level and container cgroups so that increases create headroom before container limits grow, while decreases constrain containers before shrinking the Pod-level boundary. Accurate aggregate enforcement for this v1.36 feature requires cgroup v2.

Adopting cgroup version 2

Here's what you need to use cgroup v2 with Kubernetes. First up, you need to be using a version of Kubernetes with support for v2 cgroup management; that's been stable since Kubernetes v1.25 and all supported Kubernetes releases include this support.

  • You need at least one Linux node; cgroup is a Linux-only concept
  • Your OS install must run with cgroup v2 enabled
  • The kernel version must be 5.8 or later (5.9 or later is recommended when using memory QoS)
  • The container runtime must support cgroup v2. For example:
    • containerd v1.4 or later supports cgroup v2; use containerd v2.0 or later for automatic cgroup-driver discovery

For now, you can opt back in to use cgroup v1; the Kubernetes project recommends using cgroup v2, but in Kubernetes 1.36 (the current release) the cgroup v1 option remains supported as a fallback. That fallback is scheduled for removal in Kubernetes v1.38. If you are running an older cluster, plan to migrate; if you are setting up a new cluster with Linux nodes, you should prefer cgroup v2. In either case, review both the Kubernetes runtime documentation and (if relevant) the containerd compatibility matrix.

kernel updates around cgroup v2

When Kubernetes was first announced, in 2014, only v1 cgroup existed. Version 2 cgroup management first appeared in Linux kernel 4.5, released in 2016.

  • In Linux 4.5, the cgroup v2 , , and controllers were supported.
  • Linux 4.15 added support for the cgroup v2 controller.
  • The Kubernetes project does not recommend using cgroup v2 with a Linux kernel older than 5.2 due to lack of cgroup-level task freezer support.
  • Kubernetes documents 5.8 as the minimum kernel version for cgroup v2; the root cgroup's system-level file was added in Linux 5.8.
  • The livelock fix used by Memory QoS is present in Linux 5.9 and later.
  • was added in Linux 5.19.

cgroup driver configuration

If you use to manage your cluster, Kubernetes recommends that you use the cgroup driver, because manages the kubelet as a systemd service. For other management tooling, check the documentation for the tool you're using to manage your cluster.

If you can pick either option, I recommend using the systemd driver.

Whatever tooling you've chosen, the kubelet automatically tries to detect the runtime's recommended cgroup driver. This automatic detection relies on using a runtime that implements the CRI RPC (for example: containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+).

If you're using a container runtime that supports cgroup v2 but doesn't support automatic cgroup driver detection, you can manually configure an override by editing the kubelet configuration file. For example:

Automatic discovery of the runtime's cgroup driver through the CRI, tracked by KEP-4033, graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.34. It requires a runtime that implements the CRI RPC (containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). When available, the kubelet uses the value reported by the runtime instead of its configured value.

Tools and commands that you should know about cgroups:

  • stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/: Check whether cgroup v2 is enabled; it returns .
  • systemctl list-units 'kube*' --type=slice or : List Kubernetes-related units that systemd currently has in memory.
  • bpftool cgroup list /sys/fs/cgroup/*: List all programs attached to the cgroup CGROUP.
  • systemd-cgls /sys/fs/cgroup/*: Recursively show control group contents.
  • : Show top control groups by their resource usage.
  • tree -L 2 -d /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice: Show Pods' related cgroups directories.

How to check if a Pod CPU or memory limit is successfully applied to the cgroup file?

Work from the API object down to the node. Identify the node, then compare desired resources in the spec with the enacted values in status (in-place resize can leave those out of sync):

On that node, as root, with the systemd cgroup driver and cgroup v2 (these snippets also need ). Pin the container with kubelet labels; a container name alone is not unique on a node. Use if the container is not running:

Do not treat info.runtimeSpec.linux.cgroupsPath as a filesystem path when the runtime uses the systemd driver; that value is a systemd unit path (), not a directory under .

Expected mapping at each layer:

  • Kubernetes: spec.containers[*].resources (desired) and status.containerStatuses[*].resources (enacted after in-place resize). Pod-level resources are on and the parent pod slice.
  • CRI (kubelet → runtime; these protobuf names stay cgroup v1-style even on v2): , , , , plus for Memory QoS. does not show these names; it shows the OCI spec the runtime derived from them.
  • OCI spec: linux.resources.cpu.{shares,quota,period}, linux.resources.memory.limit, and . The runtime converts shares, quota, and period into cgroup v2 files. After upgrading crun or runc, the shares-to-weight formula may change; see CPU weight conversion.
  • systemd scope: , , , . Unlimited or unset values often appear as or infinity.
  • cgroupfs: (from CPU request; an unset request still yields the default of 2 shares), , and on the container scope. Memory QoS adds , , and .

items.title: Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap
items.content:
Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost.

The Kubernetes ecosystem has reached a fundamental physical resource constraint: the strict limits of hardware memory versus the growing demand for dynamic, bursty workloads in the new agentic era.

Historically, administrators provisioning memory-intensive workloads encountered a persistent dilemma: set memory limits too high and you waste expensive infrastructure on idle RAM; set them too low and you risk Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kills.

This conflict is amplified when deploying autonomous AI agents using secure execution environments like the framework. These agentic pods require large memory footprints to initialize and execute untrusted code. However, after their burst of activity, they typically enter long-tail idle phases waiting for user prompts. Keeping this idle state in physical RAM caps cluster density and makes AI infrastructure expensive to run.

The solution: Kubernetes node swap

With the introduction of Kubernetes' support for running nodes with swap enabled (which reached General Availability in v1.34), this paradigm shifts. By enabling the Linux kernel to page out anonymous memory to disk, acts as a shock absorber during traffic spikes or periods of heavy memory oversubscription.

Historically, swap was discouraged in Kubernetes for two reasons. The first was memory accounting. Under cgroup v1, the controls treated memory and swap as a single combined limit rather than letting operators set an independent limit for disk swap. Without independent tracking, a process could page large amounts of anonymous memory out to disk, which made a container's real memory usage unpredictable and hard to isolate. Kubernetes' swap support resolves this by relying on cgroup v2, whose separate swap accounting tracks disk swap on its own. The second reason was the latency penalty of paging to slow spinning disks, which fast NVMe Local SSDs largely eliminate. Together, these make it practical to increase pod density and buffer against memory spikes without sacrificing cluster stability.

To quantify the performance boundaries and cost-saving potential of Local SSD-backed node swap, this analysis covers three distinct workload categories: a Traditional Build Workload for CI/CD pipelines, High-Density Browser Sandboxes, and Isolated Python Sandboxes.

Baseline Capacity (No Swap)

1. Traditional workload: Linux kernel build

Before exploring specialized agentic architectures, swap was validated against classic batch workloads by running a complete Linux 6.1.1 kernel build. The kernel compilation process leverages concurrent worker threads, balloons in memory to hold compiled object files, and requires a large memory spike during the brief linking phase.

This workload mirrors the memory behavior of enterprise CI/CD pipelines. Because earlier compiled objects sit inactive in memory while the pipeline progresses, CI/CD jobs frequently hoard unused physical RAM, which makes them well suited to node swap compression.

On a baseline node without swap, the minimum memory limit to prevent an OOM crash during compilation was 600 MB. Routing swap to a Local SSD cut the container memory limit by 50% to 300 MB without incurring any execution slowdown (in fact, it ran cleanly in 374s vs the baseline 433s). However, as an explicit tradeoff, compressing the limit further to 200 MB forced the active working set into swap, causing long I/O wait times and increasing execution time by over 40%. This reinforces that swap serves as an insurance policy for burst memory, not a replacement for active RAM.

2. High-density agent workloads: headless browser runtimes

AI agent workloads frequently require manipulating headless browsers via Chromium. However, trusting external code execution often requires stricter security isolation than standard Linux namespaces. This benchmark cross-evaluated several container runtime environments. The raw logs and testing methodologies for the default runtime are available in the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap directory.

  • Unsandboxed baseline limits (): To test the limits of the environment without the overhead of security runtimes, plain runc containers were swept on a c4-standard-32 node (32 vCPU, 120 GB RAM). Without swap, the node exhausted physical memory and failed past 512 pods. Enabling Local SSD swap allowed the node to support 768 concurrent pods.
  • Advanced security runtimes (for example: gVisor, Kata Containers): Enabling strict security sandboxing increases memory overhead and normally reduces pod density. However, memory swap naturally absorbs this overhead penalty. Without swap, a gVisor environment hit a hard limit at 80 pods. Local SSD swap doubled that capacity, which allowed 160 concurrent gVisor pods on a single node. Similarly, Kata Containers microVMs exhausted physical RAM at 40 concurrent pods without swap, but using GCP Local SSD swap expanded this to 50 stable Kata microVMs before CPU saturation.

At these maximum densities, the per-pod latency increase is driven mainly by pods competing for CPU, not by swap I/O. An operator tuning for a specific latency target would run at a lower density than the peak numbers here and see a proportionally smaller latency cost.

3. Beyond browsers: sandboxed Python runtimes

The advantages of node swap also extend to untrusted, isolated code-execution environments. This sweep deployed simultaneous Python sandbox sessions analyzing 5 million rows of data from the MovieLens 20M dataset, requiring a ≃375 MiB resident memory footprint per execution. The in-depth scaling results and deployment code for this sweep can be reviewed in the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap Python Density directory.

Without swap, heavy concurrent bursts exhausted physical memory, causing the node to hit a hard RAM limit and fail at 80 concurrent sessions. Enabling Local SSD swap offloaded dormant anonymous memory, freeing up physical RAM and preserving the node's page cache. This allowed the node to scale to 240 concurrently isolated Python sandboxes—a 3× density improvement. As with the browser workloads, the latency rise at peak density comes mainly from the sandboxes competing for CPU rather than from swap itself.

If you manage Kubernetes infrastructure for developer environments, browser testing farms, JVM applications, or AI execution runtimes, leveraging Local SSD swap can multiply your density efficiency.

In Kubernetes v1.34+, node swap is Generally Available. You enable it via the kubelet configuration:

Pairing this upstream configuration with your cloud provider's high-speed local disk gives you dynamic memory balancing. For example, this is natively supported on Google Kubernetes Engine via Node Memory Swap configured on Local SSD profiles.

To get the benefits, configure your workloads with Burstable QoS: set your container's memory limits higher than its requests. The node automatically rations fast swap space based on idle application memory usage while keeping active processes responsive.

As the Kubernetes ecosystem transitions into the agentic era, administrators face a growing conflict between finite hardware memory limits and the bursty behavior of AI workloads. Frameworks like Agent Sandbox provide the security isolation required for running untrusted agents, but that isolation traditionally demands large amounts of idle memory overhead.

By configuring the kubelet with and routing it to Local SSDs, you can mitigate this conflict. Fast swap offloads the dormant states of idle agents, allowing you to increase pod density and node utilization on the same infrastructure without compromising security boundaries.

items.title: Arch-specific SIMD in Go
items.author: Junyang Shao and David Chase
items.content:
Since Go 1.26, we have supported an experimental SIMD API. Now in Go 1.27, we support two more architectures: and .

The new APIs can be accessed by setting when building a program. They are defined in the package.

is the lower-level infrastructure that builds on, essentially the intrinsics layer in other languages. For exotic operations that only exist on a specific architecture, users can access them by transitioning from to (via and ). For details, please refer to the simd blog post.

For readers with prior knowledge of SIMD intrinsics in other languages, you might find that our API does not directly mirror the underlying hardware instructions:

  • We give our APIs sensible names: e.g., instead of , we just call it .
  • We leave some architecture details to compiler optimizations rather than exposing them in the API: e.g., instead of _mm512_maskz_add_ps(m, x, y), we optimize into the same instruction.

These design decisions make our APIs smaller and more accessible, and they also happily make the implementation much easier.

For readers without prior knowledge of SIMD intrinsics, we hope our low-level API is a natural and pleasant journey for you.

Please share your feedback and comments. Anything about usability, performance, etc., is appreciated. The parent issue for this project is #73787.

SIMD stands for Single Instruction, Multiple Data. SIMD instructions operate on wide registers (128-bit, 256-bit, or more) containing multiple 8- to 64-bit elements, performing operations across all elements in parallel. Wider registers and parallel execution provide a significant performance boost to algorithms that can take advantage of them.

Until now, anyone who wanted to use SIMD in Go had to endure the friction of writing assembly language. The new package is here to change that.

The goal is to support as many SIMD instructions across different architectures as possible. Currently, we have , , and available. Our support has the largest API surface, covering AVX, AVX2, and many AVX-512 extensions. Our support currently covers NEON, with SVE and some SVE2 already on the way. Our support is also mostly complete, thanks to its well-defined 128-bit SIMD abstraction.

Some users might be interested in matrix extensions on certain architectures, such as AMX and SME. We haven’t fully settled on how to represent matrices effectively in Go, so they are not yet supported, but we might support them in the future.

The architecture-specific SIMD API is imported from . uses distinct struct types, such as , , or , to signal the shape and element type of each vector, and defines operations as methods on those types. At this moment, supports only fixed-width vector extensions. Scalable vector extensions like SVE and RVV will have different struct types to represent vectors. Mask types also come with vector-like shapes, e.g., .

Across different vector widths, element types, and architectures, we use the same method name whenever operations are semantically identical:

  • Regardless of vector width or architecture, element-wise addition is simply ; the type of determines which instruction to emit. Instead of 18 different function names for addition, there is only one method name.
  • When instructions on different architectures look similar at a glance but differ in edge-case behavior, we give them distinct names so differences don’t silently bite you. For example, 16-byte table lookup on () zeros the output byte when the index is negative () and wraps modulo 16 otherwise, so we call it . On NEON () and (), any out-of-range index () zeros the output byte, so we call it .
  • On , many 256-bit and 512-bit instructions operate independently within 128-bit lanes rather than across the entire register. We explicitly suffix those methods with (such as or ) to make the 128-bit lane boundary obvious.

Methods require a receiver value, which doesn’t work for creating a vector from memory or a scalar. For those, provides package-level functions named with the target vector type:

  • : In Go 1.27, loading and storing slices use the shortest names: archsimd.LoadFloat32x4(s []float32) Float32x4 and . For tail elements that may be shorter than a full vector, archsimd.LoadFloat32x4Part(s []float32) (Float32x4, int) zero-fills the remaining lanes and returns the number of elements loaded, paired with x.StorePart(s []float32) int.
  • : Fixed-size array pointers use the suffix (archsimd.LoadFloat32x4Array(y *[4]float32) and x.StoreArray(y *[4]float32)), and archsimd.BroadcastFloat32x4(v float32) broadcasts a scalar to all lanes.

Reinterpretations are type casts without any cost. SIMD algorithms frequently reinterpret bits across element types and widths.

In the Go 1.26 experiment, we implemented this with methods, which suffered from a quadratic explosion of type pairs and couldn’t generalize to width-agnostic vectors in or SVE.

In Go 1.27, we replace them with composable zero-cost conversions:

  • reinterprets a signed integer or float vector as an unsigned integer vector of the same element width (e.g., Int32x4.ToBits() -> Uint32x4), and / converts back.
  • on unsigned vectors changes the element width within the same register width. For example, if is an , then x.ReshapeToUint32s().BitsToFloat32() reinterprets the bits of as an at zero runtime cost.

Different architectures encode vector masks very differently, e.g. mask registers on AVX-512, full vector bitmasks on AVX/AVX2, NEON, and , and predicate registers on SVE. To hide this hardware detail, provides opaque types (such as ) matching each vector shape:

  • Comparisons like produce a .
  • zeros elements where is false, and (which replaces from Go 1.26) selects elements from where is true and from where is false.
  • The compiler peepholes mask operations with the surrounding instructions: on AVX-512, or compiles into a single zero-masked or merge-masked instruction; on AVX2, NEON, or , it lowers to the appropriate bitwise or blend/bitselect instruction.

Portable algorithms like inner product can easily be implemented using the portable package, as shown in the companion simd blog post. However, we still expose to tap into exotic, architecture-specific instructions that do not fit into a portable intersection API, or instructions that can simply do things faster than what provides.

On , the GFNI extension exposes GaloisFieldAffineTransform operations. Putting aside what a Galois Field is, these operations do a simple thing:

// Each element of A is interpreted as a matrix of 8 rows of vectors of 8 bits.
// Each element of x is interpreted as a vector of 8 bits.
// The b argument is likewise a vector of 8 bits.
// The result is z[i] = (A[i/8] * x[i]) + b.
//
// The matrix * and vector + follow the usual rules for linear algebra,
// but based on AND and XOR for scalar * and +
//
// Asm: VGF2P8AFFINEQB, CPU Feature: AVX512GFNI
func (x Uint8x16) GaloisFieldAffineTransform(A Uint64x2, b uint8) Uint8x16

Each 8x8 bit matrix is packed row-by-row into a single . Because any linear combination or permutation of the 8 bits within a byte can be written as an 8x8 bit matrix, this single instruction is a Swiss Army knife for byte-level bit manipulation.

For example, reversing the bit order of every byte () normally requires nibble lookup tables, masks, shifts, and ORs in SIMD. With GaloisFieldAffineTransform, we can simply multiply each byte by the 8x8 anti-diagonal identity matrix () to reverse all 8 bits of 64 bytes at a time in a single instruction:

/*
    Anti-diagonal 8x8 bit matrix (0x8040201008040201):
    [ 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 ]   [ x7 ]   [ x0 ]
    [ 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 ]   [ x6 ]   [ x1 ]
    [ 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 ]   [ x5 ]   [ x2 ]
    [ 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 ] * [ x4 ] = [ x3 ]
    [ 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 0 ]   [ x3 ]   [ x4 ]
    [ 0 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 ]   [ x2 ]   [ x5 ]
    [ 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]   [ x1 ]   [ x6 ]
    [ 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]   [ x0 ]   [ x7 ]
*/
func ReverseBits(dst, src []uint8) {
    if !archsimd.X86.AVX512GFNI() {
        // A slow fallback emulation impl, details omitted.
        slowReverseBits(dst, src)
        return
    }
    if len(src) > len(dst) {
        // Make sure src and dst are the same size
        src = src[:len(dst)]
    }
    revMatrix := archsimd.BroadcastUint64x8(0x8040201008040201)
    var v archsimd.Uint8x64
    var i int
    for i = 0; i < len(src)-v.Len()+1; i += v.Len() {
        v = archsimd.LoadUint8x64(src[i : i+v.Len()])
        v.GaloisFieldAffineTransform(revMatrix, 0).Store(dst[i : i+v.Len()])
    }
    if i < len(src) {
        v, _ = archsimd.LoadUint8x64Part(src[i:])
        v.GaloisFieldAffineTransform(revMatrix, 0).StorePart(dst[i:])
    }
}

Another example is matrix transpose. On , the permutation instructions are shaped in a non-portable way, so using is cumbersome and might incur emulations. An efficient implementation can be written more directly in . The example below transposes an 8-by-8 matrix of 32-bit integers in registers on using AVX2’s 128-bit lane-grouped interleaves (, ) and cross-lane permutations (ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped, ):

func Transpose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7 archsimd.Int32x8) (
    b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7 archsimd.Int32x8) {
    if !archsimd.X86.AVX2() {
        // A slow fallback emulation impl, details omitted.
        return slowTranspose8(a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6, a7)
    }
    /*
            LOW  HIGH
        a0: abcd efgh
        a1: ijkl mnop
        a2: qrst uvwx
        a3: 0123 4567
        a4: ABCD EFGH
        a5: IJKL MNOP
        a6: QRST UVWX
        a7: 89yz YZ$@
    */
    t0 := a0.InterleaveLoGrouped(a1) // t0 = aibj emfn
    t1 := a0.InterleaveHiGrouped(a1) // t1 = ckdl gohp
    t2 := a2.InterleaveLoGrouped(a3) // t2 = q0r1 u4v5
    t3 := a2.InterleaveHiGrouped(a3) // t3 = s2t3 w6x7
    t4 := a4.InterleaveLoGrouped(a5) // t4 = AIBJ EMFN
    t5 := a4.InterleaveHiGrouped(a5) // t5 = CKDL GOHP
    t6 := a6.InterleaveLoGrouped(a7) // t6 = Q8R9 UYVZ
    t7 := a6.InterleaveHiGrouped(a7) // t7 = SyTz W$X@

    a0 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t2) // a0 = aiq0 emu4
    a1 = t0.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t2) // a1 = bjr1 fnv5
    a2 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t3) // a2 = cks2 gow6
    a3 = t1.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t3) // a3 = dlt3 hpx7
    a4 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t6) // a4 = AIQ8 EMUY
    a5 = t4.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t6) // a5 = BJR9 FNVZ
    a6 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(0, 1, 4, 5, t7) // a6 = CKSy GOW$
    a7 = t5.ConcatPermuteScalarsGrouped(2, 3, 6, 7, t7) // a7 = DLTz HPX@

    b0 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a4) // b0 = aiq0 AIQ8
    b1 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a5) // b1 = bjr1 BJR9
    b2 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a6) // b2 = cks2 CKSy
    b3 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(0, 2, a7) // b3 = dlt3 DLTz
    b4 = a0.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a4) // b4 = emu4 EMUY
    b5 = a1.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a5) // b5 = fnv5 FNVZ
    b6 = a2.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a6) // b6 = gow6 GOW$
    b7 = a3.ConcatPermute128Scalars(1, 3, a7) // b7 = hpx7 HPX@

    return
}

When walking through the examples above, you might have a few questions:

  • What is archsimd.X86.AVX512GFNI(), and can I omit it?
  • Why is the strided loop written as i = 0; i < len(src)-v.Len()+1; i += v.Len(), instead of i = 0; i + v.Len() <= len(src); i += v.Len()?
  • Why does take 8 vector parameters rather than a struct or an array?

At first glance these choices might look like minor stylistic preferences, but each of them is chosen for an important performance or correctness reason:

  • CPU feature checks (, )

    On , we provide runtime feature checks like , , , and extension checks like or ; on , NEON is always available, and we provide checks for optional extensions like , , and . The compiler doesn’t know ahead of time whether the machine running your binary supports optional SIMD extensions. If you don’t guard your SIMD code with the appropriate feature check, your program may crash with on hardware that lacks the instruction.

    Just as importantly, CPU feature checks act as compiler optimization hints. For example, AVX-512 supports hardware merge-masking on instruction outputs. How the compiler lowers on a 128-bit or 256-bit vector depends on which CPU features are known to be available. If the code is not guarded by , the compiler must conservatively emit a vector followed by a instruction. Inside an block, however, the compiler knows AVX-512 is available and fuses the sequence into a single merge-masked AVX-512 instruction.

  • Bounds check elimination in strided loops

    How you write the loop bound determines whether the compiler’s pass can eliminate slice bounds checks inside the loop. In , the addition could theoretically overflow to a negative if were near , which prevents the compiler from proving that is always non-negative and in-bounds. Writing avoids that potential overflow, allowing the loop body to compile with zero bounds checks.

  • Keeping vectors in registers (avoiding large composite types)

    passes 8 vector parameters rather than a struct of 8 fields or an array because Go’s ABI and SSA backend currently place large composite types in memory rather than in registers (a known issue tracked at #24416). Because SIMD vectors are 16 to 64 bytes each, spilling them to the stack hurts performance much more than spilling scalar values. This applies to both function parameters and local variables, so avoid wrapping SIMD vectors inside large arrays or structs in hot loops. There are ongoing efforts to promote composite memory accesses back into registers, which have not yet landed in Go 1.27.

In Go 1.27, supports (AVX, AVX2, and AVX-512), (NEON), and (WebAssembly 128-bit SIMD) out of the box. Whether you are on an Intel/AMD machine, an server or Apple Silicon Mac (M1/M2/M3/M4), or targeting WebAssembly, you can try natively right away:

GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/...

You can also cross-test (or via Rosetta emulation on Apple Silicon) by setting :

# Run wasm SIMD tests using a WASI runtime:
GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/...

# Or run amd64 AVX2 tests on Apple Silicon via Rosetta:
GOARCH=amd64 GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test simd/archsimd/...

We’re interested in all sorts of feedback! Early users have already helped us catch bugs (such as #77582) and identify places where code generation or API ergonomics could be improved. We tried hard to pick clear, consistent names and cover the most useful instructions, but is a massive API surface and there is always room to improve.

For Go 1.28 and beyond, we are actively working on completing SVE and SVE2 support in (introducing width-agnostic scalable vector types like backed directly by hardware SVE registers and predicates) and wiring it into . We also plan to expand to additional architectures such as , , , and , improve register promotion for composite types, and continue filling in instructions and compiler optimizations based on community feedback.

items.title: Demoting i686 Windows targets to std-only
items.author: Mateusz Mikuła, Ralf Jung
items.content:
With Rust 1.100.0, the following changes to 32-bit Windows targets will happen:

  • Tier 1 host tools target will be demoted to Tier 1 host tools.
  • Tier 2 host tools target will be demoted to Tier 2 host tools.

Builds of the standard library will continue to be distributed, but host tools such as the compiler will be no longer available. as a Tier 1 target still undergoes CI testing.

To build 32-bit Windows binaries, cross-compiling from a still-supported host toolchain (such as a 64-bit Windows ones) will be required from now on.

Desktop and Server 32-bit only x86 CPUs are no longer sold for over 15 years, and general 32-bit Windows support has ended in October 2025. This means that the development platforms these targets are meant for hardly exist these days, and even if they do exist they typically aren't capable enough for development.

Even on the modern x86_64 hardware, building i686 Windows toolchains has proven to be problematic. We have encountered compiler binaries crashing when built with the i686 MSVC target, and the GNU C++ toolchain failing with OOMs during LLVM build.

Considering all these things, cross-compiling these targets from a better supported one is what we have found to be the best solution forward. As part of that, we stopped producing host tools for these targets. For the time being, the prebuilt standard library is still available, and in case of still tested on CI.

After Rust 1.100, it will no longer be possible to install toolchains on 32-bit Windows hosts. We recommend cross-compiling from a still-supported host (such as a 64-bit Windows toolchain) instead. Other 32-bit platforms are not impacted by this change.

For more details about these demotions, see RFC 3999 for demotion, and MCP 1020 for demotion.

items.title: Announcing Rust 1.99.0
items.author: The Rust Release Team
items.content:
The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.99.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via , you can get 1.99.0 with:

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel () or the nightly channel (). Please report any bugs you might come across!

Rust 1.99.0 stabilizes defining C-ABI variadic functions with "C" and "C-unwind" ABIs. Variadic functions defined this way use a variable argument list () and accept an arbitrary number of arguments. Rust could already call externally-defined variadic functions (e.g., ). With Rust 1.99, these functions can now be written in Rust itself:

The type of is , which is ABI-compatible with the C type across targets. What types can be read from a is guarded by the trait.

For more details on c-variadic functions, see the Reference. This release also stabilizes support for defining naked variadic functions with non-"C" ABIs, which must be written via inline assembly.

This release settles the safety requirements for retrieving the size and alignment on raw pointers to both (trivially safe, already possible on stable) and non- types.

This is done by stabilizing three functions:

While there are no changes to the language semantics in Rust 1.99, we have updated the documentation on to recommend against patterns that later deallocate that memory. This was done because such code was found to have problematic interactions with current and future potential compiler optimizations, and is especially problematic with the upcoming stabilization of custom allocators. Instead, or should be preferred.

This guidance also applies to other functions in the standard library.

Many people came together to create Rust 1.99.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!
